title: Daughters Who Will Never Be Mothers
author: Susan Pickard
content:
![Daughters Who Will Never Be
Mothers](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-24-at-8.55.52
---PM.png)

Why are birthrates falling? Observers on the left tend to attribute the
decline to [_material
factors_](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2021/apr/20/britain-
falling-birthrate-covid-pandemic-conservatives-removed-support-for-
parents?ref=compactmag.com), while also typically denying it is a serious
problem at all. Voices on the right tend to point the finger at abortion and
contraception, stressing the woman's duty to reproduce. In both cases, the
deeper reasons why many women don't feel able to bear replacement-level
numbers of children--or any at all--are set aside.

Germaine Greer's 1984 book _Sex and Destiny_ , although written before
childbearing went into freefall across the West, has the virtue of being
willing to explore the dilemma rather than reaching too quickly for solutions.
Greer wrote from the perspective of a pioneering feminist who realized, too
late, that she wanted children. Greer argued that modern society has
disparaged motherhood, treating it as a private matter that individual women
had to reconcile with work as best they could. Beneath this predicament, she
concluded, lay a deep cultural malaise, a sexuality from which eros had been
evacuated and a "sterile" society unable to honor the vital life force.

Critics charged Greer with romanticizing traditional societies and overlooking
the fact that for many women motherhood was never freely chosen and came at
enormous cost. But that weakness does not destroy her central insight: that
modern societies have lost not simply the desire for children, but a sense of
belonging within the cycles and limits of life itself.

One result is anti-natalism. In cultures that see meaning only in "achievement
and self-gratification," having a child is a kind of death. This extends to
all levels: aesthetically, pregnancy offends the sleek lines, flat stomachs,
and sharp hipbones expected of women, which convey a "denial of fecundity."
Psychologically, childbearing shocks women into realizing that, far from being
simply people, they have been _women_ all along. As Greer writes, "In order to
compete with men, Western woman has joined the masculine hierarchy and
cultivated a masculine sense of self. The acknowledgement of her pregnancy
means that she must step down from all that and enter the psychological
equivalent of the birth hut." New motherhood is stressful, with most women
expected both to work and to take on the lion's share of childcare. From that
point on, many find themselves "divided"--unable fully to concentrate on, or
enjoy, either work or motherhood. For many women, the compensations of
motherhood may not be enough to make up for the loss of freedom.

And why shouldn't they? For my generation, women's right to freedom was part
of the cultural atmosphere, educated as we were when the great second feminist
wave was ebbing but still frothy, powerful. We took for granted the idea that
we could have the same freedom that educated, middle-class men had long
enjoyed. They were, after all, the ones who wrote the books and made the
films. I read the existentialists ecstatically in my teenage bedroom and
empathized deliciously with Mathieu, the hero of Jean-Paul Sartre's _Age of_
_Reason_ , committed to freedom above all else, who was disgusted by the
discovery of his girlfriend's pregnancy and the prospect of a pinched
conventional life that beckoned. I felt the horror of this situation keenly.
Like Mathieu, I thrilled to the idea of being free of societal expectations,
of rejecting the bleak life of my parents. I was more than prepared to accept
the dark side of this: the burden of autonomy, the agony of writing one's own
life, the existential loneliness of it.

> "Motherhood threatened the vision we shared."

By the time I'd reached the end of my teens, several of my friends, nice
girls, had had abortions in service of this ideal. Motherhood threatened the
vision we shared. My own mother, unavoidably, had given herself entirely to
motherhood. She abandoned or delayed her own interests and self-development:
never reading a book to its end or shopping for herself. I was a teenager the
day I finally convinced her to buy something for herself. I can't remember
what she'd bought for me, but I remember vividly the green-and-blue tartan
suit with padded shoulders (it was the '80s) that she nervously carried to the
Top Shop till. But my glee collapsed to bitter disappointment when her card
was declined. Something hard came over her, as she turned away, leaving it on
the counter in a limp pile.

I knew that my mother's enormous capacity for self-sacrifice lurked in me too.
I had to fight it, or lose my own freedom. This was not "just" selfishness; it
was also loyalty. What was the point of her sacrifices if not for her only
daughter to have a different sort of life?

* * *

As the years went by, I realized there was no such thing as pure freedom and
responsibility. I was not, in the end, Mathieu, but rather a confused
composite of Mathieu and his girlfriend, Marcelle. Obstacles that lay in my
way in life were often not of my own making, nor were they capable of being
solved by the power of will alone. I got lost in feminine pursuits, such as
romance, and adopted a feminine passivity at work, meaning that my own career
was slow, winding, tortuous. Once I finally knuckled down into my role as an
academic I found its demands brutal and often daydreamed of retreating into
motherhood. In real life, however, I have no idea how other female academics
fit motherhood into their lives. How they found the space to go after those
thoughts that suddenly appear when you are leaving work, or to follow them
down every avenue, on the small chance they bear fruit, whether a child needs
your attention or not.

I was having coffee recently with two colleagues in my department, like me
women without children. Two of us acknowledged that, despite the undoubted tug
of motherhood for much of our later-childbearing years, we could not imagine
maintaining our careers with even one child. The third was fortunate in being
free of ambiguity: She had eschewed motherhood with no inner torment. There is
good reason for this: She is part of a big family and has many relatives,
including many lovely nieces and nephews.

The other two of us mourned the fact that we were not merely only children
(our own parents, for very different reasons, had also found parenthood a
challenge), but the last of our lineage. We contemplated this together,
sharing an unspoken understanding that _we have broken that sacred line_. The
thought of it sometimes keeps me up at night, staring into the void. At three
in the morning, I see a future that is weightless, thin air, empty of human
contact.

But we have our careers, precious and hard-won. We chose the responsibility of
our own existence, as thinking people, as financially independent women, over
continuing our lineage--the long line of ancestors who had patiently borne
children, who had suffered for them and in turn were justified by them, by
passing on the blazing torch of life.

> "This is not a choice women should have to face. But we do."

This is not a choice women should have to face. But we do. Greer wrestles with
its complexity. By the time she wrote _Sex and Destiny_ , Greer was mourning
the loss of her own fertility. "I still have pregnancy dreams," she said in an
[_interview_](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/opinions/2000/05/12/motherhood-
missed/75410261-9bc3-4384-b20c-fdff531370a4/?ref=compactmag.com) a few years
later, "waiting with vast joy and confidence for something that will never
happen." This grief leaves its damp traces everywhere in her book. Her bitter
existential disappointment is what, in my view, accounts for her failure to
see the traditional practices around reproduction clearly through the mists of
romanticism, and the role that domination--not choice--has always played in
women's childbearing. Because this is the big challenge; how to cultivate a
moral accountability to posterity without basing it on patriarchal domination;
how to find a place for eros without it being inseparable from traditional
notions of masculinity and femininity.

Greer warns: "Human libido is the only force which could renew the world. In
allowing it to be drawn off, regularly tapped in domestic ritual, we are
preparing the scene of our own annihilation, stupefied by myriad petty
gratifications, dead to agony and to ecstasy." But erotic agony and ecstasy
always, always across cultures and societies ends up glorifying masculine
hierarchy. Take D.H. Lawrence, whom Greer refers to approvingly. And rightly
so. I remember the shock of recognition reading Lawrence for the first time;
how men and women were vessels for masculine and feminine archetypes, as if
they were mere containers for the gods and goddesses, and through them the
cosmos itself. The world is charged with a great vital current, and the same
flame burns in both catkins and women.

I recognized too, through Lawrence, how, for women in particular, wanting to
be free and wanting to love smashed together in a terrible collision. Take
Lawrence's alter-ego, Rupert Birkin, in _Women in Love._ Whilst Birkin insists
to Ursula that he wants an equal love between men and women, he can only do so
by drawing away from practicalities into mythic metaphors: men and women
impersonal as stars, two independent beings meeting beyond the concerns of
daily life where independence in practice fails--who does the washing up, or
whose career takes precedence.

Contemporary literature abounds with examples of women struggling with the
twin imperatives to be both a person and a woman. Most illuminatingly,
[_Sheila Heti_](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2018/jun/06/motherhood-
sheila-heti-review?ref=compactmag.com) invites us in her book _Motherhood_
into her quandary, letting us feel her oscillating imperatives--self-
determination in one moment, the sadness of forgoing motherhood--opening up to
the reader the phenomenological experience of procrastination and equivocation
which extended through her thirties. This is what Simone de Beauvoir means
when she says, of the free woman, "Her vital interests are divided." Heti is
Mathieu as a woman, for whom the choice is not to abandon a pregnant
girlfriend but to abandon what she calls the "lizard brain" part of herself
that wants her to choose motherhood. She wants to outwit nature and society at
the same time: "Do not want what a _woman_ wants," she reminds herself. "You
are not a woman who wears a diamond ring, the sort of woman … who gets what
she wants from a man." Yet when her boyfriend Miles, who already has a
daughter of his own with a former partner, encourages her not to want a child
because she has better things to do with her life, she is offended and cold
towards him--obviously. _Bastard_ , thinks the reader.

Greer reminds us of the fate of the Parsees, a Bombay community chosen by the
British back in the seventeenth century to be their commercial and cultural
intermediaries. In this role, they built up the East India Company and later
playing a significant role in India's industrialization. The Parsees took on
British cultural values of individualism and self-development, placing a high
value on education, including for girls, marrying later, and taking on the
trappings of a bourgeois lifestyle. But today, the numbers of the Parsee
community are so low that they are at risk of disappearance. One reason is
that their women, too, wanted freedom.

Perhaps the Parsees sketch out the fate of our own civilization. I don't know.
Perhaps there are answers to our crisis: cheap, available childcare, a culture
of equal parenthood, more status for mothers. But sometimes solutions are
evasions, because the dilemma itself is the thing, showing us something rich
and precious and tragic about our situation.

* * *

My mind, dwelling on such things, is apt to turn them suddenly into little
images. One such is a vision of finding a little pocket _in_ time, but not
_of_ time, a sort of underwater cave, sealed off from the rhythms of night and
day, the inexorable ticking of the clock. I see myself dwelling here, living a
whole life as a mother, and then when I'm done, returning to my life and
picking it up again. I will have lost no time, broken nothing unfixable. That
is the only way I can envision being both a mother and myself.

Meanwhile, in the real world, this dilemma brings suffering and regret, even
as it cannot easily be solved. I look at my one, faded sepia photograph of my
grandmother as a young woman, and think about all she endured as spirited
working-class woman at the turn of the last century: a pregnancy out of
wedlock during the First World War, when it was a social outrage; a husband,
later in life, with whom she was very happy, and who was killed in World War
II, along with the illegitimate son who had grown up to be so brilliant and
brave as a fighter pilot; my father, who lost his father and older half-
brother, and whose internal wounds later bore the poisonous blooms of serious
illness and disability as an adult. And then me, her only granddaughter, who
finally achieved social mobility, who built a life filled with books and ideas
but paid her back in a terrible way--by ending the line. Lying awake at night,
I find the irony almost unbearable.

Sheila Heti has another, kinder, way of thinking about this. Recognizing that
her primary female identification is as a daughter, not a mother, she says
this: "Art is written for one's ancestors … Children are eternity forwards. My
sense of eternity is backwards through time." I do not know how we can go from
being a society of daughters to one in which women choose to see themselves as
mothers, too. But on my good days, I think that finding eternity backwards
through time may itself be something good and true.
